overview: Graph Search (DFS+BFS) 4 skills test karta hai: valid traversal order identify karna, DFS edge-classification aur structural properties (discovery/finish times, connected components), BFS ki shortest-path-tree property, aur time/space complexity.
whyItMatters: 23 PYQs, aur MST (Prim's), Shortest Path, Topological Sort — sab DFS/BFS ke variations hain.
coreConcept: DFS = 'jitna deep jaa sakte ho jaao, phir backtrack karo' (stack/recursion based). BFS = 'level-by-level phailo' (queue based). DFS se 4 tarah ke edges classify hote hain: TREE (traversal ka part), BACK (ancestor की taraf), FORWARD (descendant ki taraf, non-tree), CROSS (koi relation nahi, different subtree/branch).
hinglishExplanation: DFS ko ek 'maze explore karne wala' socho jo ek raasta pakadta hai aur jitna door ja sakta hai jaata hai, dead-end pe wapis (backtrack) aata hai. BFS ek 'ripple in water' hai — source se ek ring phailti hai, phir agli ring, phir agli — isliye BFS GUARANTEED shortest path (edge-count me) deta hai unweighted graph me, DFS nahi deta.
formalDefinition: DFS: O(V+E) with adjacency list, O(V²) with adjacency matrix. BFS: same complexity, computes shortest path (in edge count) from source in unweighted graphs.
importantProperties: DFS edge types (directed graph, using discovery/finish times d[u],f[u]): TREE edge (u,v): v discovered via u. BACK edge (u,v): v is an ANCESTOR of u in the DFS tree (d[v]<d[u]<f[u]<f[v]). FORWARD edge (u,v): v is a DESCENDANT of u, but not a tree edge (d[u]<d[v]<f[v]<f[u]). CROSS edge (u,v): neither ancestor nor descendant (intervals don't overlap: f[v]<d[u]).
For UNDIRECTED graphs, DFS produces ONLY tree edges and back edges — NO forward or cross edges are possible (a key simplification vs directed graphs).
BFS tree gives the SHORTEST PATH (fewest edges) from the source to every reachable vertex in an UNWEIGHTED graph — DFS tree does NOT have this guarantee.
Number of connected components in an undirected graph = number of DFS (or BFS) calls needed to visit all vertices = number of separate trees in the DFS/BFS forest.
In a DFS forest with n vertices and c connected components, the forest has exactly n-c tree edges (each tree with k vertices has k-1 edges, summed across c trees).
DFS time = O(V+E) with adjacency LIST; O(V²) with adjacency MATRIX (because checking all possible neighbors of each vertex costs O(V) regardless of actual edge count).

formulas.forestEdgeCount: Tree edges in DFS/BFS forest = n - c (n=vertices, c=connected components)
formulas.backEdgeInterval: Back edge (u,v): d[v] < d[u] < f[u] < f[v] (v is ancestor of u)
formulas.forwardEdgeInterval: Forward edge (u,v): d[u] < d[v] < f[v] < f[u] (v is descendant of u, non-tree)
formulas.crossEdgeInterval: Cross edge (u,v): intervals [d,f] of u and v don't overlap at all

keyPropertiesAndIdentities: Undirected graph DFS: ONLY tree + back edges exist (no forward, no cross) — this is because in an undirected graph, if there were a 'forward-looking' edge from an ancestor to descendant, it would already have been discovered AS a tree edge or back edge from the other direction.

BFS tree edges always connect a vertex to another at EXACTLY one greater BFS-level/distance — any non-tree edge in a BFS traversal connects vertices whose levels differ by at most 1 (in undirected graphs) — a key property for verifying/reasoning about BFS trees.
commonPitfalls: Assuming DFS tree also gives shortest paths — only BFS guarantees this (in unweighted graphs).
Trying to classify forward/cross edges in an UNDIRECTED graph — they simply don't exist there, only tree/back edges do.
Using O(V+E) complexity even when the graph is given as an adjacency MATRIX — that representation forces O(V²) regardless of actual edge sparsity.
Miscounting connected components from tree-edge count — remember it's n-c, so c = n - (tree edges), not the other way confused.
standardTechniques: For 'valid traversal order' questions: simulate DFS (using a stack/recursion, visiting neighbors in the stated order — often alphabetical/index order unless specified) or BFS (using a queue) explicitly on the given graph.
For edge-classification questions: compute discovery and finish times via an explicit DFS simulation, then apply the interval-overlap rules above.
For BFS shortest-path-property questions: reason level-by-level — the BFS tree naturally encodes shortest distances via each vertex's level.
For connected-components questions: count how many separate DFS/BFS trees are needed to cover the whole vertex set, or apply the n-c edge-count identity directly.
